ball.q: George Eastham refused to play for Newcastle in 1960 and took an ordinary job while he fought them. Selling what?
ball.a: Cork

ball.q: Pele hated the nickname when he got it at school. What was it a mangling of?
ball.a: Bile, a goalkeeper his father's team had

ball.q: Why was the teenage Ronaldo listed as Ronaldinho in Brazil's 1994 World Cup squad?
ball.a: The squad already had an older Ronaldo, so he became the little one

ball.q: Which Manchester United defender had already won two All-Ireland football medals with Dublin?
ball.a: Kevin Moran

ball.q: Tony Cascarino won 88 caps for the Republic of Ireland. What did he later reveal in his autobiography?
ball.a: That he had never been eligible, his mother had been adopted so there was no blood link

ball.q: Which Equatorial Guinea striker, once capped by Spain at youth level, was top scorer at the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations?
ball.a: Emilio Nsue

ball.q: Diego Forlan's family had been at the top of Uruguayan football for three generations. Doing what?
ball.a: His father Pablo played at World Cups and his grandfather managed Uruguay

ball.q: Which Tottenham goalkeeper quit football at 25 saying he was bored, and went into finance?
ball.a: Espen Baardsen

ball.q: Which Manchester United winger left for Colombia in 1950 and came back known as the Bogota Bandit?
ball.a: Charlie Mitten

ball.q: Leeds City were expelled from the Football League in 1919 over illegal payments. How were their players got rid of?
ball.a: They were auctioned off in a Leeds hotel

ball.q: Manchester City's team was broken up in 1906 for illegal payments. Which club signed four of them, including Billy Meredith?
ball.a: Manchester United

ball.q: Swindon Town won the 1990 play-off final and still did not go up. Why not?
ball.a: They were punished for illegal payments and had the promotion taken away

ball.q: Tottenham were docked 12 points and thrown out of the FA Cup in 1994. What became of that punishment?
ball.a: Overturned at arbitration, so they played and reached the semi-final

ball.q: Fiorentina went bust in 2002 and were refounded in the lower leagues. What name were they forced to play under?
ball.a: Florentia Viola, until they bought the old name back

ball.q: Napoli went bankrupt in 2004. Under what name did Aurelio De Laurentiis's refounded club play at first?
ball.a: Napoli Soccer

ball.q: Parma were declared bankrupt in 2015 and restarted in Serie D. How long did it take them to get back to Serie A?
ball.a: Three seasons, with three straight promotions

ball.q: Aldershot went out of business in March 1992 with the season unfinished. What happened to their results?
ball.a: They were expunged from the table as if the games had never happened

ball.q: George Reynolds built Darlington a 25,000 seat stadium while they sat in the fourth tier. How did that end?
ball.a: The club went into administration and he was later jailed for tax fraud

ball.q: Portsmouth won the FA Cup in 2008 and were in the fourth tier by 2013. Who bought the club that year?
ball.a: Its supporters' trust, then the biggest fan owned club in England

ball.q: 1860 Munich lost a play-off in 2017 and then dropped two divisions rather than one. Why?
ball.a: Their investor refused to pay the licence fee, so they were put into the fourth tier

ball.q: Airdrieonians went bust in 2002. How did the new Airdrie United get a place in the Scottish league?
ball.a: They bought Clydebank and renamed them

ball.q: MK Dons handed back Wimbledon's trophies and honours in 2007. Who did they give them to?
ball.a: The London Borough of Merton

ball.q: Long before Milton Keynes, Wimbledon's owner pushed to move the club to another country. Which city?
ball.a: Dublin

ball.q: Charlton supporters set up a political party in 1990 to force the council's hand over The Valley. What was it called?
ball.a: The Valley Party

ball.q: Brighton sold the Goldstone Ground in 1997 and then played home games where for two seasons?
ball.a: At Gillingham, about 70 miles away

ball.q: Robert Maxwell tried in 1983 to merge Oxford United and Reading into one club. What was it to be called?
ball.a: Thames Valley Royals

ball.q: Assem Allam tried to rename Hull City. What name did he want, and who blocked it?
ball.a: Hull Tigers, blocked by the FA

ball.q: German rules would not let a drinks company put its name on a club. So what does the RB in RB Leipzig officially stand for?
ball.a: RasenBallsport, meaning lawn ball sports

ball.q: Red Bull took over Austria Salzburg in 2005 and rewrote the colours and the history. What did the old supporters do?
ball.a: Founded their own SV Austria Salzburg and started again at the bottom

ball.q: Inter were forced into a merger in 1928 under the Fascist regime. What were the club called afterwards?
ball.a: Ambrosiana, later Ambrosiana-Inter

ball.q: Fascist Italy banned English words in club names. What was Genoa Cricket and Football Club made to call itself?
ball.a: Genova 1893 Circolo del Calcio

ball.q: Franco's Spain banned foreign words in club names. What did Athletic Club have to call itself?
ball.a: Atletico Bilbao

ball.q: Barcelona and Real Madrid both had Di Stefano signed in 1953. What compromise did the Spanish federation propose?
ball.a: That he would alternate seasons between the two clubs

ball.q: Austria's Matthias Sindelar did not join the unified German team and was found dead in 1939. What was the given cause?
ball.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty flue in his flat

ball.q: England's players gave the Nazi salute before a match in Berlin in 1938. What was the score?
ball.a: England won 6-3

ball.q: Italy wore black instead of blue against hosts France at the 1938 World Cup. What did they do before kick off?
ball.a: Gave the fascist salute to the Paris crowd

ball.q: Three rounds of the 1939-40 Football League season were played before war was declared. What happened to them?
ball.a: The season was abandoned and every result expunged

ball.q: In December 1976 the Athletic Bilbao and Real Sociedad captains walked out carrying a flag that was still banned. Which flag?
ball.a: The ikurrina, the Basque flag

ball.q: Which dictator's son bought his way into Serie A with Perugia in 2003 and managed one substitute appearance?
ball.a: Muammar Gaddafi's son Al-Saadi

ball.q: Which Chilean striker refused to shake Pinochet's hand and appeared in the No campaign ads in 1988?
ball.a: Carlos Caszely

ball.q: Shakhtar Donetsk left the Donbass Arena in 2014 and did not return. Why, and where did they go?
ball.a: The war in the Donbas, so they played in exile, first in Lviv

ball.q: Which Barcelona great played international football for three different countries?
ball.a: Ladislao Kubala, for Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Spain

ball.q: Honved were abroad when the 1956 Hungarian uprising was crushed. What did the team do next?
ball.a: Toured on regardless, ending in South America, a tour FIFA refused to recognise

ball.q: Cuba have several times gone home from the Gold Cup with a smaller squad than they arrived with. Why?
ball.a: Players defect during the tournament

ball.q: Oleg Blokhin managed Ukraine at the 2006 World Cup while holding what other job?
ball.a: A seat in the Ukrainian parliament, so he had to take the job unpaid

ball.q: Which Tottenham hero of the 1981 FA Cup final did not play in the 1982 final, and why?
ball.a: Ricky Villa, because Britain and Argentina were at war over the Falklands

ball.q: Manchester United players who stayed loyal to the players' union in 1909 posed for a famous photo under what name?
ball.a: The Outcasts FC

ball.q: Scotland's referees went on strike in 2010. How were the weekend's fixtures covered?
ball.a: Referees were flown in from abroad

ball.q: English league football vanished from television for half of the 1985-86 season. Why?
ball.a: The league and the broadcasters could not agree on money

ball.q: Brazil banned women from playing football by law. In which year was the ban imposed?
ball.a: 1941, and it stood for close to forty years

ball.q: FIFA officials were arrested in a Zurich hotel in May 2015. How were they hidden from the cameras on the way out?
ball.a: Hotel staff held up bedsheets around them

ball.q: FIFA's Chuck Blazer rented a second flat in Trump Tower. What was it for?
ball.a: His cats

ball.q: Jack Warner tried to prove FIFA was persecuting him by waving an article from which website?
ball.a: The Onion, a satirical site

ball.q: A comedian gatecrashed a Sepp Blatter press conference in 2015. What did he throw over him?
ball.a: A handful of fake banknotes

ball.q: Sepp Blatter was re-elected FIFA president in May 2015. How long did he then stay in the job?
ball.a: Four days, before announcing he would go

ball.q: FIFA's own hired ethics investigator Michael Garcia quit in 2014. Why?
ball.a: FIFA published a summary of his report that he called incomplete and erroneous

ball.q: Sepp Blatter suggested in 2004 that women's football would draw bigger crowds if the players did what?
ball.a: Wore tighter shorts

ball.q: Sepp Blatter said in 2011 that racism on the pitch should be settled how?
ball.a: With a handshake at the final whistle

ball.q: Qatar went back on its promise of beer at 2022 World Cup stadiums. How long before the tournament started?
ball.a: Two days

ball.q: Nicklas Bendtner was fined heavily and banned by UEFA at Euro 2012. What had he done?
ball.a: Shown a sponsor's name on his underpants after scoring

ball.q: A South Africa against Senegal World Cup qualifier had to be played again. Why?
ball.a: The referee was banned for life for manipulating the first game

ball.q: Apartheid South Africa offered FIFA an all white team for one World Cup and an all black team for the next. What came of it?
ball.a: It was turned down and they were suspended

ball.q: Australia were said to be under a witch doctor's curse from a 1969 qualifier in Mozambique. Who claimed to lift it in 2004?
ball.a: The Australian comedian John Safran

ball.q: Israel play their football in Europe. Which confederation threw them out, and why?
ball.a: The AFC, in 1974, after member nations refused to play them

ball.q: Scotland qualified for the 1950 World Cup and did not go. What was their reason?
ball.a: They had said they would travel only as British champions, and England finished above them

ball.q: Uruguay are the only World Cup holders never to defend the trophy. Why did they stay at home in 1934?
ball.a: In revenge for the European nations who had snubbed their 1930 tournament

ball.q: Which country is the only World Cup host ever to have had to qualify for its own tournament?
ball.a: Italy, in 1934

ball.q: Which country had to play a World Cup qualifier in Rome three days before the 1934 finals kicked off?
ball.a: The United States

ball.q: Which monarch personally picked his country's squad for the 1930 World Cup and got the players time off work?
ball.a: King Carol II of Romania

ball.q: Austria qualified for the 1938 World Cup and never kicked a ball there. What had happened?
ball.a: The country had been annexed by Germany, so the team no longer existed

ball.q: Three Sheffield Wednesday players were jailed in 1965 and banned for life for betting on their own side to lose. Name one.
ball.a: Tony Kay, Peter Swan or David Layne

ball.q: Bruce Grobbelaar won a libel action over match fixing claims. What were his damages cut to at the final appeal?
ball.a: One pound, and he was left with the costs

ball.q: Two Premier League matches were abandoned in the late 1990s when the floodlights went out. What was behind it?
ball.a: A betting syndicate rigging the lights to freeze the score

ball.q: A Brazilian referee was exposed as a fixer in 2005. What happened to the eleven league games he had taken charge of?
ball.a: They were annulled and played again

ball.q: After a violent 1985 cup final the Bulgarian state dissolved CSKA and Levski. Which young forward was banned for life?
ball.a: Hristo Stoichkov, though the ban was later lifted

ball.q: A 2018 Belgian investigation into fixing and agents' money was given what name?
ball.a: Operation Clean Hands

ball.q: A Portuguese fixing investigation of 2004 was named after a golden object. Which one?
ball.a: A whistle, the Apito Dourado case

ball.q: An SPL commission examined Rangers' undisclosed payments in 2013. What did it decide about the titles they had won?
ball.a: They kept them, and the club was fined instead

ball.q: Joey Barton was banned from football in 2017 for betting. How many bets was he charged over?
Kolo Toure was banned for six months in 2011 after taking what?
ball.a: His wife's diet pills

ball.q: Maradona was thrown out of the 1994 World Cup after a failed test. What did he say had been done to him?
ball.a: That they had cut off his legs

ball.q: Ronaldinho spent five months in custody and house arrest in 2020. In which country, and what for?
ball.a: Paraguay, over a false passport

ball.q: Real Madrid wiped out enormous debts in 2001 by selling what?
ball.a: Their old training ground, rezoned by the city for office towers

ball.q: Barcelona sold off chunks of future income in 2022 so they could register players. What did they call these deals?
ball.a: Levers, palancas in Spanish

ball.q: Sandro Rosell resigned as Barcelona president in 2014 over what?
ball.a: The concealed true cost of signing Neymar

ball.q: Barcelona were accused in 2020 of paying a company to run social media accounts doing what?
ball.a: Attacking their own players and other critics of the board

ball.q: Barcelona were revealed in 2023 to have paid millions of euros over many years to which man?
ball.a: Jose Maria Enriquez Negreira, a vice president of the refereeing committee

ball.q: Massimo Cellino was barred from running Leeds United over unpaid import duty on what?
ball.a: A yacht

ball.q: Barcelona put UNICEF on the front of their shirt in 2006. What was odd about the deal?
ball.a: Barcelona paid UNICEF, instead of being paid to wear a sponsor

ball.q: Sunderland put a clause in Stefan Schwarz's 1999 contract banning one particular activity. What?
ball.a: Travelling into space

ball.q: Adrian Mutu failed a cocaine test at Chelsea and was later ordered to pay the club damages. Roughly how much?
ball.a: About 17 million euros

ball.q: Bahrain beat Togo 3-0 in a friendly in 2010. What was wrong with the opposition?
ball.a: It was a fake team with no connection to Togo, assembled by a match fixer

ball.q: A Moldovan teenager called Masal Bugduv made a newspaper list of the best young players in 2009. What was the problem?
ball.a: He did not exist, the whole player was an internet hoax

ball.q: Which Brazilian club got into the Guinness book for going almost four years without a win?
ball.a: Ibis Sport Club of Recife

ball.q: A 2002 second tier match was abandoned because Sheffield United were down to six men. Who was their manager?
ball.a: Neil Warnock

ball.q: Coventry against Bristol City in 1977 kicked off late and finished with both sides passing it about. Why?
ball.a: The Sunderland score went up on the board, and a draw kept them both up

ball.q: Luton Town began the 2008-09 League Two season on what points total?
ball.a: Minus 30

ball.q: A Hampshire referee punched a player during a Sunday league game in 1998. What did he do next?
ball.a: Showed himself the red card and walked off, leaving someone else to finish the game

ball.q: Scottish referee Dougie McDonald resigned in 2010 after admitting what?
ball.a: That he had lied about why he reversed a penalty decision

ball.q: Antonio Rattin was sent off against England in 1966 by a referee who spoke no Spanish. What reason was given?
ball.a: The look on his face, what the referee called violence of the tongue

ball.q: Julio Grondona ran Argentine football for 35 years wearing a ring engraved with which two words?
ball.a: Todo pasa, everything passes
